name: Ideal Gas Law (solve for P)
description: Solves the ideal gas law for pressure as amount of substance times the gas constant times absolute temperature divided by volume. With 2 mol at 300 K in 0.05 m³ the pressure is about 99,768 Pa.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (kelvin) and volume in cubic meters, giving pascals with R=8.314. The ideal gas law is an approximation, most accurate at low pressure and high temperature.

name: Ideal Gas Law (solve for V)
description: Solves the ideal gas law for volume as amount of substance times the gas constant times temperature divided by pressure. It gives the volume a gas sample occupies under the stated conditions.
notes: Temperature in kelvin and pressure in pascals with R=8.314 give volume in cubic meters. Accuracy is best for dilute gases far from condensation; real gases deviate at high pressure.

name: Ideal Gas Law (solve for T)
description: Solves the ideal gas law for temperature as pressure times volume divided by amount of substance times the gas constant. The result is the absolute temperature in kelvin.
notes: Pressure in pascals and volume in cubic meters with R=8.314 give kelvin. The result is absolute temperature; subtract 273.15 to convert to degrees Celsius.

name: Ideal Gas Law (solve for n)
description: Solves the ideal gas law for the amount of substance as pressure times volume divided by the gas constant times temperature. The result is the number of moles of gas present.
notes: Pressure in pascals, volume in cubic meters, and temperature in kelvin with R=8.314 give moles. Multiply by molar mass to convert moles to a mass.

name: Boyle's Law (solve for P2)
description: Applies Boyle's law to find the new pressure of a gas after its volume changes at constant temperature, as initial pressure times initial volume divided by final volume. Halving the volume doubles the pressure.
notes: Volumes must share the same unit; temperature and amount of gas are held constant. Pressure and volume are inversely proportional only when the process is isothermal.

name: Charles's Law (solve for V2)
description: Uses Charles's law to find a gas's new volume after a temperature change at constant pressure, as initial volume times final temperature divided by initial temperature. Volume is proportional to absolute temperature.
notes: Temperatures must be absolute (kelvin), not Celsius, or the ratio is wrong. Holds at constant pressure with a fixed amount of gas.

name: Gay-Lussac's Law (solve for P2)
description: Applies Gay-Lussac's law to find a gas's new pressure after a temperature change at constant volume, as initial pressure times final temperature divided by initial temperature. Pressure is proportional to absolute temperature.
notes: Temperatures must be in kelvin, not Celsius, for a correct ratio. Valid at constant volume with a fixed amount of gas.

name: Combined Gas Law (solve for P2)
description: Uses the combined gas law to find a gas's final pressure when both volume and temperature change, as initial pressure times initial volume times final temperature divided by initial temperature times final volume. It merges Boyle's, Charles's, and Gay-Lussac's laws.
notes: Temperatures must be absolute (kelvin); volumes must share a unit. Assumes a fixed amount of gas and ideal behavior throughout the change.

name: Sensible Heat (Q = m·c·ΔT)
description: Computes the heat needed to change a substance's temperature without changing its phase, as mass times specific heat capacity times the temperature change. Heating 2 kg of water by 20 K needs about 167,440 J.
notes: Use consistent SI units: mass in kilograms, specific heat in J/(kg·K), temperature change in kelvin (equal to a Celsius change). Applies only within a single phase, not during melting or boiling.

name: Latent Heat (Q = m·L)
description: Calculates the heat absorbed or released during a phase change at constant temperature, as mass times the specific latent heat. Melting 0.5 kg of ice needs about 167,000 J.
notes: Mass in kilograms and latent heat in J/kg give joules. Use the latent heat of fusion for melting or freezing and of vaporization for boiling or condensing; temperature stays constant during the change.

name: Specific Heat Capacity (c)
description: Determines a material's specific heat capacity by dividing the heat added by the product of its mass and its temperature rise. It quantifies the heat required to raise one kilogram by one kelvin.
notes: Heat in joules, mass in kilograms, temperature change in kelvin give J/(kg·K). Valid for a single phase with no phase change; the temperature change must be nonzero.

name: Linear Thermal Expansion (ΔL)
description: Computes how much a solid's length changes with temperature, as the linear expansion coefficient times the original length times the temperature change. A 10 m bar with coefficient 1.2×10⁻⁵ per K warmed 50 K grows about 6 mm.
notes: The coefficient is per kelvin, original length in meters, and temperature change in kelvin, giving the length change in meters. This is a small-change linear approximation; a negative change means contraction on cooling.

name: Area Thermal Expansion (ΔA)
description: Calculates the change in surface area of a material when its temperature changes by dT. It multiplies twice the linear expansion coefficient by the original area A0 and the temperature change, giving the area increase in the same square units as A0.
notes: Uses the small-expansion approximation where the area coefficient equals about 2 times the linear coefficient, so it is accurate only for modest temperature changes. Coefficient must match the material and temperature unit (per K).

name: Volume Thermal Expansion (ΔV)
description: Gives the change in volume of a substance heated or cooled by dT. It multiplies the volume expansion coefficient beta by the original volume V0 and the temperature change, returning the volume increase in the same cubic units as V0.
notes: For isotropic solids beta is roughly 3 times the linear coefficient. The formula is a first-order approximation valid for small temperature changes and assumes beta is constant over that range.

name: Heat Conduction Rate (Fourier)
description: Computes the steady-state rate of heat flow through a slab by Fourier's law: thermal conductivity k times cross-sectional area A times the temperature difference dT, divided by thickness L. The result is the conducted power in watts.
notes: Assumes steady state, one-dimensional conduction and a uniform material with no internal heat sources. Thickness L is measured along the heat-flow direction; k depends on the material.

name: Stefan-Boltzmann Radiated Power
description: Calculates the thermal radiation power emitted by a surface using the Stefan-Boltzmann law: emissivity times the constant sigma times surface area A times absolute temperature to the fourth power. The result is radiated power in watts.
notes: Temperature T must be absolute (kelvin) because it is raised to the fourth power, so small errors are strongly amplified. This gives gross emission; net radiative exchange requires subtracting absorbed power from the surroundings.

name: Heat Engine Efficiency
description: Gives the maximum (Carnot) efficiency of a heat engine operating between two reservoirs: one minus the ratio of the cold reservoir temperature Tc to the hot reservoir temperature Th. The result is a dimensionless fraction between 0 and 1.
notes: Both temperatures must be absolute (kelvin). This is the ideal upper limit for a reversible engine; real engines always fall below it. Multiply by 100 to express as a percent.

name: Carnot Refrigerator COP
description: Computes the ideal coefficient of performance of a Carnot refrigerator: the cold reservoir temperature Tc divided by the difference between the hot and cold temperatures. It expresses how much heat is removed from the cold space per unit of work input.
notes: Temperatures must be absolute (kelvin). The COP can exceed 1 and grows large as Th approaches Tc. This is the reversible upper limit; real refrigerators perform worse.

name: Carnot Heat Pump COP
description: Gives the ideal coefficient of performance of a Carnot heat pump: the hot reservoir temperature Th divided by the difference between the hot and cold temperatures. It shows how much heat is delivered to the warm space per unit of work input.
notes: Temperatures must be absolute (kelvin). The heating COP is always the refrigerator COP plus 1 and always exceeds 1. This is the reversible ideal; real heat pumps deliver less.

name: RMS Speed of Gas Molecules
description: Calculates the root-mean-square speed of molecules in an ideal gas: the square root of three times the gas constant R times temperature T divided by molar mass M. The result is a characteristic molecular speed in meters per second.
notes: Molar mass M must be in kilograms per mole and temperature T in kelvin. RMS speed differs from the mean and most-probable speeds; it is the speed tied to average kinetic energy.

name: Average Kinetic Energy per Molecule
description: Gives the average translational kinetic energy of a single gas molecule: three halves of the Boltzmann constant kB times the absolute temperature T. The result is the mean energy per molecule in joules and depends only on temperature.
notes: Temperature T must be in kelvin. This counts only translational motion (three degrees of freedom) and does not include rotational or vibrational energy of polyatomic molecules.

name: Speed of Sound in Ideal Gas
description: Computes the speed of sound in an ideal gas: the square root of the adiabatic index gamma times the gas constant R times temperature T divided by molar mass M. The result is the sound speed in meters per second.
notes: Temperature T must be in kelvin and molar mass M in kilograms per mole. Gamma is about 1.4 for diatomic gases like air; the model assumes adiabatic, ideal-gas behavior.

name: Entropy Change
description: Computes the entropy change of a reservoir as the heat transferred divided by its absolute temperature, Q/T. It measures how much the system's disorder changes during the heat exchange.
notes: Valid for a reversible transfer at constant temperature; the temperature must be absolute (kelvin). Positive Q (heat in) raises entropy, negative Q lowers it.

name: COP (Heating)
description: Gives the ideal (Carnot) coefficient of performance of a heat pump in heating mode, Th/(Th - Tc), the ratio of heat delivered to work input. A smaller temperature gap yields a higher COP.
notes: This is the theoretical maximum; real heat pumps fall short. Both temperatures must be absolute (kelvin) and the hot reservoir must be warmer than the cold one.

name: COP (Cooling)
description: Gives the ideal (Carnot) coefficient of performance of a refrigerator or cooler, Tc/(Th - Tc), the ratio of heat removed from the cold side to work input. A smaller temperature gap yields a higher COP.
notes: This is the theoretical upper limit; real coolers perform below it. Temperatures must be absolute (kelvin), and the cooling COP is always the heating COP minus one.

name: Thermal Efficiency
description: Computes the thermal efficiency of a heat engine as 1 minus the ratio of rejected heat to input heat, 1 - Qc/Qh. It is the fraction of input heat converted into useful work.
notes: The result is a fraction between 0 and 1; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Both heats are magnitudes in the same energy unit, and rejected heat cannot exceed input heat.

name: Carnot Efficiency
description: Gives the maximum possible efficiency of any heat engine operating between two temperatures, 1 - Tc/Th. It sets the theoretical ceiling that no real engine can exceed.
notes: Both temperatures must be absolute (kelvin); using Celsius gives wrong results. Real engines with friction and irreversibility always fall below this limit.

name: R-Value (Thermal Resistance)
description: Computes the thermal resistance (R-value) of a material layer as its thickness divided by its thermal conductivity. A higher R-value means the layer insulates better.
notes: Applies to a single homogeneous layer; combine layers by summing their R-values. Result is in SI units (m²K/W), which differ from imperial R-values by a factor of about 5.68.

name: U-Value
description: Computes the thermal transmittance (U-value) as the reciprocal of the total R-value, 1/R. It measures how readily heat passes through an assembly, so lower U-values insulate better.
notes: The input should be the total R-value of the whole assembly, not a single layer. U-value and R-value are inverses, so units must be consistent (W/m²K versus m²K/W).

name: Heat Loss Rate
description: Computes the steady-state heat loss through a building element as U-value times area times the temperature difference across it. The result is the rate of heat flow in watts.
notes: Assumes steady-state conduction and a uniform U-value over the area. The temperature difference is between the two sides; only its magnitude affects the loss rate.

name: Heating Degree Days
description: Accumulates heating degree-days as the base temperature minus the mean outdoor temperature (clamped at zero) times the number of days. It gauges how much heating demand a period has.
notes: The max(0, …) term ensures no negative contribution on days warmer than the base. Temperatures are in Celsius here, and the base temperature choice strongly affects the total.

name: Series Thermal Resistance
description: Adds the R-values of three layers in series to give the total thermal resistance of the assembly, R1 + R2 + R3. Stacked layers combine by simple addition of resistances.
notes: Valid only for layers in series (heat passing through one after another), not parallel paths. All R-values must share the same units for the sum to be meaningful.

name: Conductive Heat Flux
description: Applies Fourier's law per unit area to give the conductive heat flux through a slab, thermal conductivity times temperature difference divided by thickness. The result is power per square meter.
notes: Assumes steady-state, one-dimensional conduction through a uniform slab. This is flux (per unit area); multiply by area to get total heat flow in watts.

name: Fourier Heat Conduction
description: Computes the total conductive heat flow through a slab using Fourier's law, conductivity times area times temperature difference divided by thickness. The result is the heat rate in watts.
notes: Assumes steady-state, one-dimensional conduction through a uniform slab with fixed face temperatures. Unlike the flux form, this includes area and gives total power.

name: Ideal Gas Pressure
description: Solves the ideal gas law for pressure, P = nRT/V, from the amount of gas, temperature, and volume. It gives the pressure an ideal gas exerts under those conditions.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (kelvin) and all inputs in SI units, giving pascals. Real gases deviate at high pressure or low temperature.

name: Otto Cycle Efficiency
description: Gives the ideal thermal efficiency of the Otto cycle used in gasoline engines, one minus the reciprocal of the compression ratio r raised to gamma minus one. It shows that efficiency rises with compression ratio and with the heat capacity ratio gamma.
notes: Assumes an ideal air-standard cycle with constant gamma and no irreversibilities; real engines fall short due to friction, heat loss, and knock limits on r. The result is a fraction (multiply by 100 for percent).

name: Diesel Cycle Efficiency
description: Computes the ideal thermal efficiency of the Diesel cycle from compression ratio r, heat capacity ratio gamma, and cutoff ratio alpha. For the same compression ratio it is slightly lower than the Otto cycle because of the finite constant-pressure heat addition.
notes: Cutoff ratio alpha must exceed 1; as alpha approaches 1 the efficiency approaches the Otto value. Assumes an ideal air-standard cycle with constant gamma and no losses.

name: Brayton Cycle Efficiency
description: Gives the ideal thermal efficiency of the Brayton cycle used in gas turbines, one minus the reciprocal of the pressure ratio rp raised to (gamma minus one) over gamma. Efficiency increases with the compressor pressure ratio.
notes: Assumes an ideal air-standard cycle with constant gamma and isentropic compression and expansion; real turbines suffer component inefficiencies. The result is a fraction (multiply by 100 for percent).

name: Adiabatic Temperature (TV Relation)
description: Computes the final temperature of an ideal gas after a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) volume change, T1 times the volume ratio raised to gamma minus one. Compression (V1 greater than V2) raises the temperature, while expansion cools the gas.
notes: Applies only to reversible adiabatic processes of an ideal gas with constant gamma and no heat exchange. Temperature T1 must be absolute (kelvin) and the volumes share the same units.

name: Adiabatic Pressure (PV Relation)
description: Gives the final pressure of an ideal gas after a reversible adiabatic (no heat exchange) volume change, using P1×(V1/V2)^gamma. As the gas is compressed (V2 smaller than V1) the pressure rises faster than in an isothermal process because of the exponent gamma.
notes: Valid only for a quasi-static adiabatic process on an ideal gas with constant gamma (about 1.4 for diatomic gases). Use absolute pressures; the result carries the same pressure unit as P1.

name: Adiabatic Temperature (TP Relation)
description: Computes the final temperature of an ideal gas after a reversible adiabatic pressure change via T1×(P2/P1)^((gamma-1)/gamma). Raising the pressure raises the temperature; lowering it cools the gas, as in adiabatic expansion.
notes: Assumes an ideal gas with constant gamma and no heat transfer. Temperatures and pressures must be absolute (K and Pa); an isentropic path is implied.

name: Adiabatic Work (Ideal Gas)
description: Gives the work done by an ideal gas in a reversible adiabatic process as (P1V1−P2V2)/(gamma−1). Because no heat is exchanged, this work equals the drop in internal energy of the gas.
notes: Requires consistent SI units (Pa and m^3) so the result is in joules, and a constant gamma. A positive value means work done by the gas during expansion.

name: Isothermal Expansion Work
description: Calculates the work done by n moles of an ideal gas expanding reversibly at constant temperature, nRT×ln(V2/V1). At fixed temperature all this work comes from absorbed heat since internal energy is unchanged.
notes: Valid for a reversible isothermal process on an ideal gas; use absolute temperature in kelvin. Expansion (V2 greater than V1) gives positive work, compression gives negative.

name: Joule-Thomson Inversion Temperature
description: Estimates the maximum inversion temperature of a van der Waals gas, 2a/(Rb), above which throttling (Joule-Thomson expansion) warms the gas rather than cooling it. Below it the gas cools on expansion.
notes: This is an approximate van der Waals result using the constants a and b; real inversion temperatures depend on pressure. Keep a, R and b in consistent SI units for a result in kelvin.

name: Van der Waals Equation (Pressure)
description: Gives the pressure of a real gas from the van der Waals equation, nRT/(V−nb) − an²/V². The term nb corrects for finite molecular volume and an²/V² for intermolecular attraction, improving on the ideal gas law.
notes: Requires substance-specific constants a and b in matching SI units; V must exceed nb or the result is unphysical. Reduces to the ideal gas law when a and b are zero.

name: Redlich-Kwong Equation (Pressure)
description: Computes real-gas pressure from the Redlich-Kwong equation of state, RT/(V−b) − a/(√T·V(V+b)), for one mole. Its temperature-dependent attraction term often models gases better than van der Waals near moderate pressures.
notes: Uses molar volume and the RK constants a and b in consistent SI units; V must exceed b. The a term carries a K^0.5 factor, so temperature must be absolute (K).

name: Van der Waals Critical Temperature
description: Gives the critical temperature of a van der Waals gas, 8a/(27Rb), the temperature above which the gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone. It is set entirely by the constants a and b.
notes: Derived from the van der Waals critical point; keep a, R and b in consistent SI units for a result in kelvin. Real critical temperatures deviate somewhat from this model.

name: Van der Waals Critical Pressure
description: Gives the critical pressure of a van der Waals gas, a/(27b²), the pressure at the critical point where the liquid and gas phases become indistinguishable. It depends only on the constants a and b.
notes: Comes from the van der Waals critical point; use a and b in matching SI units so the result is in pascals. The model gives approximate values for real substances.

name: Van der Waals Critical Volume
description: Gives the critical volume of a van der Waals gas, 3nb, the total volume occupied by n moles at the critical point. It scales directly with the number of moles and the excluded-volume constant b.
notes: Based on the van der Waals critical point (molar critical volume equals 3b). Keep b in m^3/mol for a result in m^3; real critical volumes differ modestly.

name: Compressibility Factor Z
description: Computes the compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT), the ratio of a real gas volume to that predicted by the ideal gas law. Z = 1 means ideal behavior; values above or below 1 show repulsion or attraction dominating.
notes: Dimensionless; use consistent SI units and absolute temperature and pressure. Z depends on the gas, temperature and pressure, so it is not a fixed constant.

name: Newton's Law of Cooling
description: Gives an object temperature at time t while cooling toward its surroundings, Ts + (T0−Ts)·exp(−kt). The gap between object and surroundings shrinks exponentially at a rate set by the cooling constant k.
notes: Assumes a constant surrounding temperature and a rate proportional to the temperature difference; k and t must use the same time unit. Works for heating too when T0 is below Ts.

name: Convective Heat Transfer Rate
description: Computes the convective heat flow from a surface, hA(Ts−Tinf), following Newton's law of cooling. It rises with the heat transfer coefficient h, the area A, and the temperature difference between the surface and the fluid.
notes: Assumes a constant coefficient h over the area; the result is positive when the surface is hotter than the fluid. Temperature difference in K equals the difference in °C.

name: Net Radiative Heat Exchange
description: Gives the net radiative heat transfer from a gray body to its surroundings, εσA(T1⁴−T2⁴), from the Stefan-Boltzmann law. The fourth-power dependence makes radiation grow steeply with temperature.
notes: Temperatures must be absolute (K) because of the fourth power; emissivity ε is between 0 and 1. This form assumes a small body in large surroundings.

name: Isothermal Compressibility (Ideal Gas)
description: Gives the isothermal compressibility of an ideal gas, 1/P, the fractional volume decrease per unit pressure increase at constant temperature. Higher pressure makes the gas harder to compress further.
notes: Exact only for an ideal gas at constant temperature; the result has units of inverse pressure (1/Pa). Real gases deviate, especially near condensation.

name: Adiabatic Compressibility (Ideal Gas)
description: Gives the adiabatic (isentropic) compressibility of an ideal gas, 1/(γP). Because no heat escapes during compression, the gas resists compression more than isothermally, by the factor gamma.
notes: Valid for an ideal gas undergoing a reversible adiabatic change; result units are inverse pressure (1/Pa). It is always smaller than the isothermal compressibility 1/P.

name: Adiabatic Bulk Modulus (Gas)
description: Gives the adiabatic bulk modulus of a gas, γP, its resistance to compression when no heat is exchanged. This modulus also sets the speed of sound in the gas.
notes: Applies to an ideal gas under adiabatic compression; use absolute pressure so the result is in the same pressure unit. It is the reciprocal of the adiabatic compressibility.

name: Polytropic Process Work
description: Gives the work done by a gas in a polytropic process (PVⁿ constant), (P1V1−P2V2)/(n−1). The polytropic index n generalizes the adiabatic case, covering intermediate paths between isothermal and adiabatic.
notes: Uses SI units (Pa, m^3) for a result in joules and requires n not equal to 1 (the isothermal case needs a logarithmic formula). Positive work means expansion.

name: Isothermal Entropy Change (Ideal Gas)
description: Computes the entropy change of n moles of an ideal gas expanding or compressing at constant temperature, nR·ln(V2/V1). Expansion increases entropy as the gas accesses more configurations.
notes: Valid at constant temperature for an ideal gas; volumes may be in any consistent unit since only their ratio matters. Result is in J/K, positive for expansion.

name: Entropy Change on Heating
description: Gives the entropy change when a substance of mass m and specific heat c is heated from T1 to T2, mc·ln(T2/T1). Heating raises entropy; the log form reflects the 1/T weighting of added heat.
notes: Assumes constant specific heat over the range and uses absolute temperatures (K). Result in J/K is positive for heating (T2 greater than T1), negative for cooling.

name: Ideal Gas Entropy Change (T and V)
description: Computes the total entropy change of an ideal gas that changes both temperature and volume, nCv·ln(T2/T1) + nR·ln(V2/V1). It sums the thermal and the volumetric contributions to entropy.
notes: Uses the molar heat capacity at constant volume and absolute temperatures; volume ratio needs consistent units. Valid for an ideal gas with constant Cv.

name: Carnot Engine Work Output
description: Gives the maximum work a Carnot engine delivers from heat Qh drawn at the hot reservoir, Qh(1−Tc/Th). The factor (1−Tc/Th) is the Carnot efficiency, the theoretical ceiling for any heat engine between those temperatures.
notes: Reservoir temperatures must be absolute (K). This is an ideal upper bound; real engines produce less because of irreversibilities.

name: Second-Law (Exergetic) Efficiency
description: Gives the second-law efficiency, the ratio of actual thermal efficiency to the Carnot efficiency, eta_th/eta_carnot. It measures how close a real engine comes to the ideal reversible limit.
notes: Dimensionless, ranging from 0 to 1; both inputs are fractions (not percentages). A value of 1 would mean fully reversible, unattainable operation.

name: Exergy of Heat Transfer
description: Gives the exergy (maximum useful work) obtainable from heat Q supplied at temperature T with ambient T0, Q(1−T0/T). Higher source temperatures relative to the environment yield more available work.
notes: Temperatures must be absolute (K), with T above T0. Only the Carnot fraction of the heat is convertible to work; the rest is unavailable energy.

name: Final Temperature of Mixing
description: Gives the equilibrium temperature when two masses at different temperatures mix, (m1c1T1+m2c2T2)/(m1c1+m2c2). It is the heat-capacity-weighted average of the starting temperatures.
notes: Assumes an insulated system with no phase change and constant specific heats. Since it is a ratio, temperatures may be in K or °C, giving the result in the same unit.

name: Volumetric Expansion Coefficient (Beta = 3 Alpha)
description: Converts a material linear thermal expansion coefficient to its volumetric coefficient, 3α. For an isotropic solid, volume expands roughly three times as fast as a single length dimension.
notes: Valid for isotropic materials with small expansions; the factor 3 comes from expansion in all three dimensions. Both coefficients share the unit 1/K.

name: Thermal Diffusivity
description: Gives a material thermal diffusivity, k/(ρc), which governs how quickly temperature changes propagate through it. High diffusivity means heat spreads rapidly relative to how much energy the material stores.
notes: Use consistent SI units (W/(m·K), kg/m^3, J/(kg·K)) so the result is in m^2/s. It reflects transient heat conduction, not steady-state heat flow.

name: Biot Number
description: Computes the Biot number, hL/k, comparing internal conduction resistance to surface convection resistance in a solid. A value well below 0.1 means the object stays nearly uniform in temperature during heating or cooling.
notes: Dimensionless; k here is the solid conductivity and L the characteristic length (volume/surface area). Bi under 0.1 justifies the lumped-capacitance approximation.

name: Nusselt Number
description: Gives the Nusselt number, hL/kf, the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer across a fluid boundary layer. Larger values indicate convection dominates over pure conduction in the fluid.
notes: Dimensionless; kf is the fluid conductivity, distinct from any solid. A Nusselt number of 1 corresponds to heat transfer by conduction alone.

name: Log Mean Temperature Difference
description: Computes the log mean temperature difference, (ΔT1−ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2), the effective driving temperature difference for a heat exchanger. It correctly averages the difference that varies along the exchanger length.
notes: ΔT1 and ΔT2 are the end temperature differences and must both be positive and unequal. It applies to counter- or parallel-flow exchangers with constant properties.

name: Number of Transfer Units (NTU)
description: Gives the number of transfer units, UA/(m·cp), a dimensionless measure of a heat exchanger thermal size relative to the fluid heat capacity rate. Higher NTU means the exchanger can transfer heat more completely.
notes: Uses the smaller fluid heat capacity rate (mass flow times specific heat) in the denominator. Dimensionless; keep U, A, m and cp in consistent SI units.

name: Gibbs Phase Rule
description: Gives the number of degrees of freedom of a system at equilibrium, C−P+2, where C is components and P is coexisting phases. It tells how many intensive variables (like temperature and pressure) can vary independently.
notes: The constant 2 accounts for temperature and pressure; the result cannot be negative for a valid equilibrium. Additional constraints (like a reaction) would reduce it.

name: Trouton's Rule (Enthalpy of Vaporization)
description: Estimates the molar enthalpy of vaporization of a liquid from its normal boiling point using Trouton's rule, about 88·Tb. It reflects the roughly constant entropy of vaporization (~88 J/(mol·K)) for many liquids.
notes: An empirical approximation; use the boiling point in kelvin for a result in J/mol. It fails for liquids with strong hydrogen bonding, such as water and alcohols.

name: Gibbs-Helmholtz Equation
description: Estimates the Gibbs energy at temperature T2 from its value at T1, using T2·(G1/T1 + dH·(1/T2−1/T1)) from the Gibbs-Helmholtz relation. It extrapolates Gibbs energy with temperature at fixed enthalpy.
notes: Assumes the enthalpy change dH is constant over the temperature interval; use absolute temperatures (K). Accuracy drops if dH varies significantly with temperature.

name: Ideal Gas Enthalpy
description: Gives the enthalpy of an ideal gas relative to absolute zero, nCpT, using the molar heat capacity at constant pressure. For an ideal gas enthalpy depends only on temperature, not pressure or volume.
notes: Uses absolute temperature (K) and assumes constant Cp; the result in joules is measured from a 0 K reference. Only enthalpy differences are physically meaningful.

name: Mayer's Relation (Cp from Cv)
description: Gives the molar heat capacity at constant pressure from that at constant volume, Cp = Cv + R (Mayer's relation). The gas constant R is the extra energy needed for expansion work when heating at constant pressure.
notes: Holds exactly only for an ideal gas; keep Cv and R in the same molar units (J/(mol·K)). It does not apply to liquids or solids.

name: Heat Capacity Ratio (Adiabatic Index)
description: Gives the heat capacity ratio γ = Cp/Cv, also called the adiabatic index. This dimensionless value governs adiabatic processes and the speed of sound, and reflects a gas molecular degrees of freedom.
notes: Dimensionless and always greater than 1; use consistent units for Cp and Cv. Typical values are about 1.67 for monatomic and 1.4 for diatomic gases.

name: First Law of Thermodynamics (Change in Internal Energy)
description: Calculates the change in internal energy of a system using the first law of thermodynamics, based on the heat added to the system and the work done by the system on its surroundings. This is a general energy-balance relation applicable to any thermodynamic process.
notes: Uses the sign convention where heat added to the system (Qh) is positive and work done by the system (W) is positive; applies to a closed system with no change in the amount of substance.

name: Isobaric (Constant-Pressure) Work Done by an Ideal Gas
description: Calculates the work done by an ideal gas as it expands or is compressed at constant pressure. The work equals the pressure multiplied by the change in volume, and is positive for expansion and negative for compression.
notes: Valid only for a quasi-static (reversible) process at strictly constant pressure; for processes where pressure varies, this must be replaced by the integral of P dV.

name: Change in Internal Energy of a Monatomic Ideal Gas
description: Calculates the change in internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas resulting from a change in temperature. Because the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, this relation holds regardless of the process (constant volume, constant pressure, etc.).
notes: Applies specifically to monatomic ideal gases (e.g. noble gases), where only translational kinetic energy contributes; diatomic or polyatomic gases require a different numerical coefficient due to additional rotational/vibrational degrees of freedom.

name: Molar Heat Capacity at Constant Volume (Monatomic Ideal Gas)
description: Gives the molar heat capacity at constant volume for a monatomic ideal gas, derived from the equipartition theorem applied to the three translational degrees of freedom. It represents the heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of gas by one kelvin at constant volume.
notes: Applies only to monatomic ideal gases; this value is a constant that does not depend on temperature, pressure, or the amount of gas.

name: Molar Heat Capacity at Constant Pressure (Monatomic Ideal Gas)
description: Gives the molar heat capacity at constant pressure for a monatomic ideal gas, equal to the constant-volume heat capacity plus the gas constant R (Mayer's relation). It represents the heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of gas by one kelvin at constant pressure, including the work of expansion.
notes: Applies only to monatomic ideal gases; this value is a constant that does not depend on temperature, pressure, or the amount of gas.

name: Gas Pressure from Kinetic Theory (Molecular Model)
description: Calculates the pressure exerted by an ideal gas from the kinetic theory of gases, relating pressure to the number of molecules, the mass of each molecule, their root-mean-square speed, and the container volume. This links the macroscopic pressure to the microscopic motion of gas molecules.
notes: Assumes an ideal gas: point-like molecules, negligible intermolecular forces except during perfectly elastic collisions, and molecules in random, uniformly distributed motion.

name: Maxwell-Boltzmann Most Probable Speed
description: Gives the most probable molecular speed in a gas at thermal equilibrium, the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution, as the square root of 2kT divided by molecular mass m. It is the speed at which the largest fraction of molecules travel.
notes: Use the mass of one molecule in kg, not molar mass, and temperature in kelvin. This most probable speed is the smallest of the three characteristic speeds, below the mean and rms speeds.

name: Maxwell-Boltzmann Mean Speed
description: Computes the arithmetic mean speed of gas molecules at temperature T from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, as the square root of 8kT divided by pi times molecular mass m. It represents the average of the speed magnitudes of all molecules.
notes: Use molecular mass in kg and temperature in kelvin. The mean speed lies between the most probable and rms speeds, being about 1.128 times the most probable speed.

name: Maxwell-Boltzmann RMS Speed
description: Gives the root-mean-square speed of gas molecules as the square root of 3kT divided by molecular mass m. This speed corresponds directly to the mean translational kinetic energy, since half m times the rms speed squared equals three-halves kT.
notes: Use the mass of one molecule in kg and temperature in kelvin. The rms speed is the largest of the three characteristic speeds and is the physically relevant one for kinetic energy.

name: Mean Translational Kinetic Energy
description: Computes the average translational kinetic energy of a single gas molecule as three-halves times the Boltzmann constant times absolute temperature. It reflects that each of the three translational degrees of freedom carries half kT of energy.
notes: Depends only on temperature, not on molecular mass or gas identity. Temperature must be absolute (kelvin); this is energy per molecule, so multiply by Avogadro's number for a per-mole value.

name: Boltzmann Factor
description: Evaluates the Boltzmann factor, the exponential exp of minus the state energy En divided by kT. It gives the relative probability weight of a microstate at energy En in thermal equilibrium, before normalization by the partition function.
notes: En and kT must share energy units (joules here); only energy differences are physically meaningful. States far above kT in energy are strongly suppressed, while states well below are nearly equally likely.

name: Two-Level Partition Function
description: Computes the partition function of a two-level system, one plus the Boltzmann factor of the upper level with energy gap En. It sums the statistical weights of the ground and excited states and normalizes their occupation probabilities.
notes: The ground state is taken at zero energy, so its weight is 1; En is the gap in joules. At high temperature the value approaches 2 (both levels equally populated) and at low temperature approaches 1.

name: Two-Level System Average Energy
description: Gives the average energy of a two-level system with energy gap En at temperature T, En divided by the quantity exp(En/kT) plus one. It rises from zero at low temperature toward half the gap as both levels become equally populated at high temperature.
notes: Ground state is at zero energy and En is the gap in joules. The form resembles a Fermi-Dirac occupation because a two-state system can hold at most one excitation.

name: Schottky Two-Level Heat Capacity
description: Computes the heat capacity of a two-level system, the Schottky anomaly, from the energy gap En and temperature T. It exhibits a characteristic peak near kT comparable to En, where the system most readily absorbs energy by promoting particles across the gap.
notes: Result is per particle; multiply by the number of particles for a bulk value. The peak occurs around T where kT is roughly En/2.4; the capacity falls to zero at both very low and very high temperatures.

name: Equipartition Theorem Energy
description: Gives the average thermal energy predicted by the equipartition theorem, one-half kT for each of f quadratic degrees of freedom, so half f times kT total. It applies to classical systems where each such degree contributes equally to the energy.
notes: Valid only in the classical high-temperature limit where energy levels are closely spaced; quantum freezing-out at low temperature removes degrees of freedom. Count both translational and, where active, rotational and vibrational degrees in f.

name: Sackur-Tetrode Entropy (Thermal Wavelength Form)
description: Computes the absolute entropy of a monatomic ideal gas via the Sackur-Tetrode equation in thermal-wavelength form, from particle number N, volume V, and thermal de Broglie wavelength lam. It captures how entropy grows with the number of accessible quantum states per particle.
notes: Requires the dilute regime where V/(N·lam^3) is much greater than one, otherwise quantum degeneracy invalidates the formula. The 2.5 additive term comes from the ideal-gas energy and Stirling approximation.

name: Planck Single-Mode Average Energy
description: Gives the average thermal energy of a single electromagnetic mode of frequency f, the Planck occupation times the photon energy hf. It is the Bose-Einstein result that replaces classical equipartition and cures the ultraviolet catastrophe.
notes: This excludes the zero-point energy hf/2. At low frequency (hf much less than kT) it tends to kT, recovering the classical limit; at high frequency it is exponentially suppressed.

name: Maxwell-Boltzmann Occupation Number
description: Computes the classical Maxwell-Boltzmann occupation of a state with energy En and chemical potential mu, exp of minus (En minus mu) divided by kT. It gives the average number of particles in that state in the dilute, non-degenerate limit.
notes: Valid when occupation is much less than one, so quantum statistics reduce to the classical form. En and mu share energy units; states below mu are more populated, above mu less.

name: Dulong-Petit Law
description: States the Dulong-Petit law that the molar heat capacity of a simple crystalline solid is three times the gas constant R. It follows from equipartition, with each atom contributing three kinetic and three potential quadratic degrees of freedom.
notes: Holds only at high temperature, well above the Debye temperature; below it the capacity falls toward zero. The result about 24.9 J/(mol·K) is independent of the specific element.

name: Einstein Model Heat Capacity
description: Computes the molar heat capacity of a solid in the Einstein model, treating N atoms as independent quantum oscillators at a single frequency set by the Einstein temperature theta. It reproduces the Dulong-Petit value at high T and falls off toward low temperature.
notes: Assumes all oscillators share one frequency, so it underestimates the low-temperature capacity compared to the Debye T-cubed behavior. theta and T are in kelvin; the ratio theta/T is dimensionless.

name: Boltzmann Entropy Formula
description: Evaluates Boltzmann's entropy formula, the Boltzmann constant times the natural log of the number of accessible microstates W. It connects the microscopic count of equally probable configurations to the macroscopic thermodynamic entropy.
notes: W must be a pure count (dimensionless) and at least one; ln(W) grows slowly, so entropy scales with the logarithm of the enormous microstate count. Assumes all microstates are equally probable.

name: Ideal Gas Chemical Potential
description: Computes the chemical potential of a monatomic ideal gas as kT times the natural log of the number density n times the cube of the thermal de Broglie wavelength lam. It measures the energy change on adding one particle at fixed temperature and volume.
notes: In the classical dilute regime n·lam^3 is much less than one, so the logarithm is negative, giving a negative chemical potential. n is number density in 1/m^3, not moles.

name: Radiation Energy Density (Stefan-Boltzmann)
description: Gives the energy density of blackbody radiation as four times the Stefan-Boltzmann constant divided by the speed of light, times temperature to the fourth power. It is the total electromagnetic energy per unit volume inside a cavity at temperature T.
notes: Scales steeply with the fourth power of temperature, so doubling T raises the density sixteenfold. Temperature must be absolute (kelvin); this is the integrated density over all wavelengths.

name: Rayleigh-Jeans Law
description: Evaluates the Rayleigh-Jeans spectral radiance, two times the speed of light times kT divided by the fourth power of wavelength lam. It is the classical approximation to blackbody radiation, accurate only at long wavelengths.
notes: Diverges as wavelength shrinks (the ultraviolet catastrophe), so it fails at short wavelengths where Planck's law is required. Valid only when hc/lam is much less than kT.

name: Planck's Law (Spectral Radiance, Wavelength)
description: Computes the spectral radiance of a blackbody per unit wavelength at wavelength lam and temperature T, via Planck's law. It gives the power emitted per unit area, per unit solid angle, per unit wavelength, peaking at a wavelength set by Wien's law.
notes: Wavelength lam is in meters and T in kelvin; the result is per unit wavelength, differing from the per-frequency form. It reduces to Rayleigh-Jeans at long wavelengths and Wien's form at short wavelengths.

name: Planck's Law (Spectral Radiance, Frequency)
description: Computes the spectral radiance of a blackbody per unit frequency at frequency nu and temperature T, via Planck's law. It gives the emitted power per unit area, per unit solid angle, per unit frequency across the thermal spectrum.
notes: This per-frequency form is not simply the wavelength form divided by lam; the two peak at different points. Frequency nu is in Hz and T in kelvin; only positive temperatures are physical.

name: Mean Free Path (Ideal Gas)
description: Estimates the average distance a gas molecule travels between collisions, kT divided by the square root of two times pi times the square of the molecular diameter times pressure. It shows how the mean free path shrinks with higher pressure and larger molecules.
notes: Treats molecules as hard spheres of diameter d and uses the square-root-of-two factor for relative motion. Pressure P is in pascals and T in kelvin; the path grows with temperature at fixed pressure.

name: Molecular Collision Frequency
description: Computes how many collisions a single gas molecule undergoes per second, the square root of two times pi times the square of the molecular diameter times the mean speed times the number density. It links molecular size, speed, and crowding to collision rate.
notes: Uses the hard-sphere collision cross-section with the square-root-of-two factor for relative velocities. n is number density in 1/m^3 (not moles) and vmean the mean molecular speed in m/s.

name: Debye T-Cubed Heat Capacity
description: Gives the low-temperature molar heat capacity of a solid in the Debye model, proportional to the cube of the ratio of temperature to the Debye temperature theta. It captures how lattice vibrations freeze out, driving the capacity to zero as T cubed.
notes: Valid only well below the Debye temperature, typically T less than about theta/10; near or above theta it overestimates and the full Debye integral is needed. T and theta are in kelvin.

name: Langevin Function (Paramagnetism)
description: Evaluates the Langevin function coth(x) minus 1/x, written here with exponentials, describing the classical mean magnetic alignment of dipoles. The argument x is the ratio of magnetic to thermal energy, mu·B divided by kT, and the output ranges from 0 to 1.
notes: For small x it rises linearly as x/3 (Curie law); for large x it saturates toward 1 as dipoles fully align. The coth form has a removable singularity at x=0, so avoid exactly zero input.

name: Entropy of Mixing (Binary)
description: Computes the entropy of mixing for a binary system of N particles with mole fraction x of component A, minus N k times (x ln x plus (1 minus x) ln(1 minus x)). It quantifies the entropy gained when two ideal components are mixed at random.
notes: Mole fraction x must lie strictly between 0 and 1; the entropy is always positive and peaks at x equal to 0.5. Assumes ideal mixing with no interaction energy between components.

name: Quantum Harmonic Oscillator Partition Function
description: Computes the canonical partition function of a quantum harmonic oscillator of frequency f at temperature T, including the zero-point energy in the numerator. It sums the Boltzmann weights over the evenly spaced energy ladder of the oscillator.
notes: The numerator exp(-hf/2kT) reflects the zero-point energy; dropping it shifts the energy origin. At high temperature the value grows as kT/hf, recovering the classical limit.

name: Quantum Harmonic Oscillator Mean Energy
description: Gives the mean thermal energy of a quantum harmonic oscillator of frequency f, the zero-point energy hf/2 plus the Planck occupation times hf. It shows how the oscillator's energy exceeds the classical kT value at low temperature due to zero-point motion.
notes: Includes the zero-point term, so the energy never drops below hf/2 even at absolute zero. At high temperature (kT much greater than hf) it approaches the classical kT.

name: Radiation Pressure (Photon Gas)
description: Computes the pressure exerted by isotropic blackbody radiation, four times the Stefan-Boltzmann constant divided by three times the speed of light, times temperature to the fourth power. It equals one third of the radiation energy density for a photon gas.
notes: Scales with the fourth power of absolute temperature, becoming significant only at very high temperatures such as stellar interiors. Assumes an isotropic photon gas in thermal equilibrium.

name: Ideal Gas Internal Energy (Equipartition)
description: Computes the internal energy of n moles of an ideal gas from equipartition as half f times n times the gas constant R times temperature, where f is the number of active quadratic degrees of freedom per molecule. It gives the total translational and, where relevant, rotational and vibrational energy.
notes: Use f=3 for monatomic, 5 for diatomic at moderate temperature, and more when vibration activates. Valid in the classical regime; quantum modes may be frozen out at low temperature.

name: Density of States (3D Free Electron Gas)
description: Computes the density of states of a three-dimensional free electron gas at energy En in volume V, scaling with the square root of energy. It gives the number of available electronic states per unit energy, a key input for Fermi-gas and solid-state calculations.
notes: This form excludes the factor of two for spin degeneracy; multiply by 2 if spin is counted. Uses the reduced Planck constant hbar and electron mass m in SI units, with energy En in joules.

name: Helmholtz Free Energy from Partition Function
description: Computes the Helmholtz free energy of a system from its canonical partition function Z at temperature T, as F=-k×T×ln(Z), using Boltzmann's constant. It links the microscopic partition function to a macroscopic thermodynamic potential.
notes: Z is the dimensionless canonical partition function and must be positive; temperature T is in kelvin. A larger Z (more accessible microstates) gives a more negative, lower free energy.

name: Radiation between Two Parallel Grey Plates
description: Gives the net radiant heat flux between two large parallel grey surfaces.
notes: Shiny surfaces (low ε) block radiation — the idea behind reflective insulation.

name: Enthalpy of Moist Air
description: Gives the enthalpy of humid air per kilogram of dry air (ASHRAE), the basis of psychrometric load calculations.
notes: Differences in enthalpy give total (sensible + latent) coil loads.

name: Pendulum Clock Daily Error from Temperature
description: Gives how many seconds per day a pendulum clock loses when its rod warms and lengthens (negative = losing).
notes: Why precision clocks used invar or compensated pendulums.

name: Isentropic Efficiency of a Compressor
description: Compares the ideal temperature rise with the actual one; for an ideal gas it equals the ratio of ideal to actual work.
notes: Good centrifugal compressors reach 80–88 %.

name: Isentropic Efficiency of a Turbine
description: Compares the actual temperature drop across a turbine with the ideal (isentropic) drop.
notes: Large gas turbines reach about 90 %.

name: Compressor Work per kg (Isentropic, Ideal Gas)
description: Gives the ideal work to compress one kilogram of gas adiabatically between two pressures.
notes: Divide by the isentropic efficiency for the real work.

name: Curzon–Ahlborn Efficiency (Engine at Maximum Power)
description: Gives the efficiency of a heat engine run for maximum power rather than maximum efficiency (Curzon and Ahlborn 1975).
notes: Often closer to real power plants than the Carnot limit.

name: Combined Cycle Efficiency
description: Gives the overall efficiency when the waste heat of one engine (a gas turbine) drives a second (a steam cycle).
notes: Modern combined-cycle plants exceed 60 %.

name: Polytropic Exponent from Two States
description: Gives n in pVⁿ = constant from two measured states of a compression or expansion.
notes: n = 1 isothermal, n = γ adiabatic; real engines lie in between.

name: Van der Waals Constants from Critical Point
description: Gives the van der Waals attraction constant a from a gas's critical temperature and pressure; b = RT_c/(8p_c).
notes: CO₂ gives a ≈ 0.366 Pa·m⁶/mol².

name: Van der Waals Volume Constant b from Critical Point
description: Gives the van der Waals excluded-volume constant b from critical temperature and pressure.
notes: CO₂ gives b ≈ 4.28 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol.

name: Compressibility Factor from the Second Virial Coefficient
description: Gives Z = pV/(nRT) from the truncated virial equation, good for moderately dense gases.
notes: Negative B (attraction dominates) makes Z below 1.

name: Heat to Turn Ice into Steam
description: Adds up the heat to warm ice to 0 °C, melt it, heat the water to 100 °C, boil it and heat the steam, at atmospheric pressure.
notes: Boiling (2257 kJ/kg) takes over 5 times the heat of warming water from 0 to 100 °C.

name: Entropy Generated by Mixing Hot and Cold Water
expression: m1 * c * ln(tf / t1) + m2 * c * ln(tf / t2)
description: Gives the total entropy change when two amounts of water mix; it is always positive — the second law in a cup.
notes: Find the final temperature first from energy balance.

name: Joule–Thomson Temperature Drop
description: Estimates the temperature change of a gas throttled through a valve: μ_JT times the pressure drop.
notes: Air at room temperature cools about 0.25 K per bar; hydrogen warms (it is above its inversion temperature).

name: Stirling Engine Power (Beale Number)
description: Estimates the shaft power of a Stirling engine from the empirical Beale number (about 0.15 for well-designed engines).
notes: A quick first sizing, not a design method.

name: Heat Flow through a Pipe Wall
expression: 2 * pi * k * l * (ti - to) / ln(r2 / r1)
description: Gives the steady conduction heat flow through the wall of a cylinder, such as pipe insulation.
notes: Doubling the insulation thickness does not halve the loss: the logarithm softens it.

name: Heat Flow through a Spherical Shell
description: Gives steady conduction through a hollow sphere, such as the insulation of a spherical tank.
notes: A negative value means heat flows inwards.

name: Critical Insulation Radius (Cylinder)
description: Gives the outer radius at which adding insulation to a thin wire or pipe first stops increasing its heat loss.
notes: Thin electrical cables often lose more heat with insulation than without.

name: Straight Fin Efficiency
expression: tanh(sqrt(2 * h / (k * t)) * l) / (sqrt(2 * h / (k * t)) * l)
description: Gives the efficiency of a thin rectangular fin with an insulated tip: the heat it sheds relative to an ideal fin at base temperature throughout.
notes: Aluminium heat-sink fins are typically 80–95 % efficient.

name: Lumped-Capacitance Cooling Time
expression: rho * v * c / (h * a) * ln((t0 - tf) / (t - tf))
description: Gives the time for a small or highly conductive object (Biot number < 0.1) to cool to a target temperature.
notes: Check the Biot number first; otherwise temperatures inside differ.

name: Thermal Time Constant
description: Gives the time for a small body to cover 63 % of the gap to its surroundings' temperature; five time constants is about 99 %.
notes: Sets how fast a thermometer or sensor responds.

name: Counterflow Heat Exchanger Effectiveness
description: Gives the fraction of the maximum possible heat a counterflow exchanger transfers (ε-NTU method).
notes: For C_r = 1 use ε = NTU/(1 + NTU).

name: Parallel-Flow Heat Exchanger Effectiveness
description: Gives the effectiveness of a parallel-flow (co-current) exchanger; it is always below the counterflow value.
notes: Can never exceed 1/(1 + C_r).

name: Rayleigh Number
description: Gives the Rayleigh number, which decides whether natural convection is laminar (below about 10⁹ on a vertical plate) or turbulent.
notes: For air β ≈ 1/T.

name: Natural Convection on a Vertical Plate (Churchill–Chu)
description: Gives the average Nusselt number on a vertical heated plate, valid for all Rayleigh numbers (Churchill and Chu 1975).
notes: h = Nu·k/L.

name: Radiation Heat Transfer Coefficient
description: Linearises radiation exchange into an equivalent heat transfer coefficient, so it can be added to convection.
notes: Around room temperature it is about 5–6 W/(m²·K) — similar to still-air convection.

name: Ice Thickness Growth (Stefan's Law)

variables.label: Degrees below freezing at the surface

description: Gives the thickness of ice formed on still water after time t with a constant air temperature below freezing (Stefan 1891).
notes: Growth slows with time: four times as long gives only twice the thickness.

name: Contact Temperature of Two Touching Bodies
description: Gives the interface temperature when two semi-infinite bodies touch, weighted by their thermal effusivity √(kρc).
notes: Why metal (high effusivity) feels colder than wood at the same temperature.

name: Thermal Effusivity
description: Gives a material's thermal effusivity, which sets how warm or cold it feels to the touch.
notes: Wood about 400, skin about 1800, steel about 14,000.

name: Penetration Depth of a Temperature Change
description: Estimates how deep a temperature change at the surface reaches into a solid after time t.
notes: Daily temperature swings reach only about 10–20 cm into soil; yearly ones a few metres.

name: Surface Temperature under Constant Heat Flux (Semi-Infinite Solid)
expression: ti + 2 * q * sqrt(al * t / pi) / k
description: Gives the surface temperature of a thick solid heated by a constant flux, rising with the square root of time.
notes: Used for laser, welding and brake-disc heating estimates.

name: Heat Loss by Air Infiltration
description: Gives the heating power lost to air leaking or ventilated out of a building (0.33 W·h/(m³·K) for air).
notes: Heat-recovery ventilation can return 70–90 % of it.

name: Convective Heat Transfer Coefficient of Wind on a Surface
description: Gives the McAdams estimate of the outside convective coefficient of a building surface or solar collector in wind.
notes: A common simple correlation; values vary widely with surface and direction.

name: Pipe Heat Loss per Metre with Insulation and Convection
description: Gives the heat lost per metre of an insulated pipe, adding the insulation and outside-air resistances in series.
notes: Bare steel pipe loses several times more.
